definition: Nurture means to care for something and help it develop.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word nurture. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know nurture should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Bakers nurture a sourdough starter for years, feeding it by the clock and guarding it from drafts.
Tend is milder than nurture — tending covers the basic chores, water the plant, feed the cat, with no promise of anything more, while nurture aims every feeding at growth.
Coddle goes further than nurture — nurture builds strength toward independence, while coddling protects so completely that nothing ever toughens.

Raise means to bring up a child or an animal until it is grown — the word is tied to that job and ends when the growing-up does. Nurture travels wider and needs no finish line: you can nurture a talent, a friendship, or a project, adjusting the care daily so it develops.

To look after something is to keep it safe and fed — the sitter looks after the dog, and success is nothing going wrong. Nurture aims past looking after: nurture points the same care at growth, at helping the thing become more than it was.

The owlet came to the raptor center as a fist of wet feathers.

The staff nurtured her by hand: tweezer-fed at first, then glove-fed; they warmed her box at night, moved her to a flight cage sized to her wingspan, and hid live mice in the straw so that hunting could grow at the pace her wings did.
Nurture is the exact word for that year of care, because nurture means to care for something and help it develop — the feeding and the growing belong together.
Protect is only half of it: a protected owl stays alive; a nurtured one learns to hunt.
Nurture is the hands-on member of the caring family: feeding, warming, adjusting, daily.
Foster, its unit-mate, arranges conditions from a step back; cherish holds a thing dear without needing it to grow at all.
If there is a feeding schedule and the goal is growth, nurture is the word.

Rook's Corner was never really a chess club; it was a greenhouse for players.
Adeyemi did more than teach openings.
He watched how each child lost, then chose their next opponent the way a gardener chooses where the light falls.
A shy girl got quiet endgame puzzles until her patience became a weapon.
A reckless boy was given faster clocks, then slower ones, until his daring learned discipline.
Parents sometimes asked why he never simply drilled the rules.
'Rules keep a player safe,' he said.
'I am not here to keep them safe.' He did not guard talent; he nurtured it — care aimed at growth, adjusted week by week, with no finish line in sight.
